relation_proposals.evidence_context: Surface runoff develops when water flows over the land, including when rainfall exceeds the ground's ability to absorb it or when the ground is already saturated. Gravity moves runoff downslope toward channels, streams, and rivers. A watershed is the land area that drains surface water toward a common outlet. Rivers carry water downstream, while lakes and wetlands can temporarily store it and influence the timing of its movement. Snow and ice also store water; melting releases liquid water that can enter streams or soil. Storage and movement occur over different timescales, so water does not follow one compulsory loop. A water budget compares inputs, outputs, and changes in storage within a defined area and time interval. Human activities can alter this balance. Paved surfaces often reduce infiltration and increase rapid runoff. Pumping removes groundwater, and sustained withdrawals greater than replenishment can reduce groundwater storage. Understanding these pathways helps explain how rainfall, underground reserves, and downstream water availability are connected.
